bib.title: Codified Context: Infrastructure for AI Agents in a Complex Codebase

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 9 pages, 45,366 of 45,366 chars, including the references and Appendices A and B. No extraction faults. The PDF contained no embedded instructions. Page numbers below are inferred from the running headers, so treat them as approximate.

SOURCE: "Codified Context: Infrastructure for AI Agents in a Complex Codebase", Aristidis Vasilopoulos (independent researcher, sole author). It is a preprint, arXiv:2602.20478v1 [cs.SE], 24 Feb 2026, and the paper calls itself "a systems paper and experience report" (p5).

CORE CLAIM: Single-file manifests (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) do not scale to a ~100k-line codebase. The paper proposes a three-tier "codified context" setup that treats documentation written for agents as load-bearing infrastructure:
- Tier 1 is a hot-memory "constitution", about 660 lines, always loaded. It holds conventions, build commands, checklists, known failure modes, and trigger tables that route file areas to agents.
- Tier 2 is 19 domain-specialist agent specs. More than half of each spec is project-domain knowledge.
- Tier 3 is a cold-memory knowledge base of 34 subsystem specs, served on demand through a keyword-matching MCP server with five search tools.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (single developer, single project, Claude Code only, no baseline):
- Project: a 108,256-line C# real-time multiplayer game (MonoGame and an ECS library), built over 283 sessions in 70 part-time days, with 148 commits (Table 3, p5).
- Context infrastructure: 54 files and about 26,200 lines, which is 24.2% of the code size. By tier: constitution 0.6%, agents 8.6%, knowledge base 15.0%. The author says the ratio "reflects this project's complexity and domain, not a target or finding".
- Interaction data comes from 1,457 JSONL conversation files, a snapshot with some early files lost. Agent-chain data covers only a 31-day window.
  - 2,801 human prompts, 1,197 agent invocations and 16,522 agent turns, about 6 autonomous turns per prompt.
  - Of 757 classifiable invocations, 432 (57%) were project specialists.
  - More than 80% of prompts were 100 words or fewer.
  - Prompts about the infrastructure itself were 4.3% of substantive prompts.
  - About 87% of sessions were ad hoc and about 13% followed a plan-execute-review flow.
- The knowledge base saw 1,478 MCP retrieval calls across 218 sessions.
- Maintenance cost is self-reported: about 5 minutes per session when a spec is touched, plus a biweekly review of 30-45 minutes, averaging 1-2 hours per week.
- The four case studies were selected for qualitative diversity, and each is one anecdote:
  - Save system: `save-system.md` was used in 74 sessions, and the author reports "no save-related bugs".
  - UI sync: the next feature applied the documented pattern on the first attempt.
  - Drop system: a retrieval query returned zero results, which exposed an undocumented subsystem.
  - Deterministic RNG: the network-protocol-designer agent (about 915 lines, about 65% domain knowledge) found three bugs that had eluded five prior attempts.

QUOTES:
1. "single-file manifests (.cursorrules, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md) do not scale beyond modest codebases" (p1-2).
2. "The constitution answers 'what rules must you always follow?'; Tier 3 answers 'how does subsystem X work in detail?'" (p3).
3. "Agents trust documentation absolutely and out-of-date specs cause silent failures" (p6, guidelines). The paper also says "Specification staleness was the primary failure mode" (p7).
4. "No causal relationships are claimed; confounding factors including developer experience growth cannot be isolated." (p4)

Useful related-work figures that the paper cites from others and did not measure:
- AGENTS.md presence was associated with a 29% reduction in median runtime and 17% in output tokens (Lulla et al. 2026, arXiv:2601.20404).
- Only about 5% of 466 surveyed repos had adopted a context file.
- 72.6% of Claude Code manifests specify architecture.

LIMITS:
- There is no baseline, no ablation of the tiers, and no controlled benchmark. The paper names controlled benchmarking as future work.
- It covers one developer, one project, and one tool (Claude Code with MCP). The author's background is chemistry, and the domain is unusually documentation-heavy. Transfer to teams and to other project types is untested.
- The metrics describe usage, not correctness. The outcome claims are anecdotal and self-reported, and the author is also the sole judge.
- Data are partial: lost early logs and a 31-day window for agent chains.
- No model versions are given. The paper also says an initial draft was prepared with AI assistance.
- The keyword substring retrieval is basic. Embedding retrieval is deferred.
- The context drift detector is described, but no results are given for it.
- A claim of "redundant encoding" for routing compliance is not measured.

BUILDS ON:
- Empirical studies of manifest files: Chatlatanagulchai et al. 2025 (arXiv:2509.14744 and 2511.12884).
- Agentic Context Engineering, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2510.04618). It supplies the "brevity bias" idea, which the paper uses to justify embedding domain knowledge in agent specs.
- Mei et al. 2025, a survey of context engineering (arXiv:2507.13334).
- Google Conductor 2026, a concurrent system.
- MCP (Anthropic 2025).
- Hong et al., MetaGPT, 2023, for the idea that rich structured context primes agents.
- Cemri et al. 2025 (arXiv:2503.13657) and the planner-coder gap study (arXiv:2510.10460), for multi-agent failure.

The "docs as infrastructure for agents" idea has no single credited origin.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p3), "Three-tier codified context infrastructure". It shows the always-loaded constitution, trigger-table-routed specialist agents, and the cold knowledge base queried through MCP. A second option is Figure 4 (p6), the six practitioner guidelines (G1-G6).

FIT: It is on topic but weak evidence. It is a good practitioner illustration of the hot/cold split, routing tables, and keeping docs in sync with code (stale specs, drift detector). Cite it as an experience report, not as proof that the pattern works.

CODE (spec format worth quoting, p4): the Tier 3 doc template uses "Known Failure Modes" symptom, cause and fix tables. Appendix B shows an agent frontmatter with `name`, `description`, `tools` and `model`, and a "READ-ONLY for diagnostics" marker.
